The availability of such tariffs will create a compelling market demand, driving innovation and reducing costs. Programs like the expanded dynamic pricing pilots21 and the California Energy Commission’s CalFlexHub22 are valuable resources in aiding in this near-term capability development. The business models for price responsive capabilities remain a significant unknown. While our study considered the cost of communication hardware and software subscriptions for past demand response-enabling technologies, the actual pricing structures that will be offered by manufacturers or automation service providers are still largely undetermined. Some may include these features at no cost to increase product appeal, while others may have discrete cost structures requiring upfront and/or monthly payments. Additionally, service providers and utilities could enter agreements where the savings achieved through price response are shared at set percentages, which would impact the savings that are then able to be passed on to customers. At the most basic level, the annual revenue potential estimated in this study can be compared to a typical up-front cost of a BESS. As shown in Section 3.5, batteries responding to dynamic prices would be encouraged to charge and discharge 1-3 times per day, depending on the price design and season. On the low end, large C&I customers may only earn a few dollars a year per kWh of battery capacity on a Mild tariff (low price forecast scenario). The most lucrative dynamic price for batteries (PG&E residential price, high price forecast scenario, Full dynamic tariff design) would earn customers $67 per year per kWh of battery capacity. As a ballpark, a 13.5 kWh Tesla Powerwall costs customers around $10,000 to install, coming out to $740/kWh. This means the BESS would be paid off in 11 years of fixed dynamic prices, not accounting for maintenance and management costs, discounting of future savings, or financing the BESS purchase. The payback period for using batteries solely to take advantage of dynamic price fluctuations is relatively long, making this a less attractive proposition for most customers. Current BESS installations tend to be motivated by other factors, however. In areas prone to outages or grid instability, the ability to maintain power during critical events is often valued more than potential savings from price arbitrage. Customers are also motivated by the desire to become more energy self-sufficient, especially those with rooftop solar. These users often install batteries to store excess solar generation during the day, which they can use during the evening or in the event of an outage.
